documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

Paul is a 68 y/o retired man joining us from another primary care office. Brought every bottle in a grocery bag as asked.

Cardiac history: MI in Feb 2020, taken to the cath lab at a regional hospital, one drug-eluting stent to the LAD. Since then he gets a pressure in the middle of his chest a few times a month, walking up the hill on his street with the dog or carrying bags of mulch. Stops, it goes away in a couple of minutes. Pattern unchanged over the last year. No rest pain, no syncope, no palpitations, no orthopnea. Sees outside cardiology yearly; last there this spring.

Other: BP treated for close to ten years. Cholesterol on atorvastatin since around the same time. Knees ache after gardening, both sides, worse on stairs; acetaminophen a couple of times a week does the job. Never had injections.

Meds (bottles reviewed): aspirin 81 daily, atorvastatin 40 qhs, metoprolol succinate 50 daily, lisinopril 20 daily, acetaminophen 500 q6h prn. Takes them all; uses a weekly pill box.
Allergies: NKDA.

PMH/PSH: as above. Colonoscopy 2018 normal per outside records.
FH: father MI at 62. Mother had high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes. Brother has coronary disease.
SH: retired, divorced, lives alone with his dog; daughter lives nearby and checks in. Smoked about a pack a day for 25 years, quit 2015. Alcohol 1-2 drinks a week, usually beer with the football game. Walks the dog every morning, big vegetable garden.

ROS: no weight change, no GI bleeding, no urinary trouble, mood good. PHQ-2 0.

Exam: Well appearing, pleasant. BP 134/82, HR 62. Lungs clear. Heart regular, no murmur. No JVD. Abdomen soft, no bruit, no pulsatile mass. Extremities without edema, pedal pulses 2+. Knees with bony enlargement and crepitus bilaterally, no effusion, full extension. Neuro grossly intact.

A/P:
1. CAD s/p MI and LAD stent 2020, chronic stable angina: symptoms stable and infrequent. Continue aspirin, atorvastatin 40, metoprolol. Will get last cardiology note.
2. HTN: at goal-ish today, continue lisinopril 20. BMP today.
3. Hyperlipidemia: lipid panel today on atorvastatin 40.
4. OA knees: acetaminophen prn, fine as is.
5. Former smoker, 25 pk-yr, quit 6 yrs ago: discussed lung cancer screening, he'd like to do it. Low-dose CT ordered. One-time aortic ultrasound ordered.
6. Health maintenance: PCV20 today. Hep C screen with labs. A1c (mother with DM). Flu shot next month when the high-dose arrives. Colonoscopy UTD (2018).

RTC 4 months, sooner prn.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Paul, your labs from Tuesday look good. Kidney function, potassium and liver tests are normal, blood count normal, A1c is in the normal range so no sign of diabetes, and the hepatitis C screen is negative. LDL cholesterol on the atorvastatin is close to what your old office had. The CT scheduling office will call you about the lung scan and the aorta ultrasound. Nice to have you with us.

reports.study: Low-dose CT chest for lung cancer screening
reports.text:
LOW-DOSE CT CHEST, LUNG CANCER SCREENING (BASELINE)
Indication: 68-year-old former smoker, 25 pack-years, quit 2015.
Technique: Low-dose helical CT of the chest without IV contrast.
Comparison: None.
Findings: Lungs: No pulmonary nodules. No consolidation or emphysema. Airways patent. Pleura: No effusion or thickening. Mediastinum: No lymphadenopathy. Heart normal in size. Coronary artery calcification, with a stent in the left anterior descending artery. Thoracic aorta normal in caliber. Upper abdomen: unremarkable. Bones: degenerative change in the thoracic spine.
reports.conclusion: Lung-RADS 1: negative. Continue annual screening with low-dose CT in 12 months. Coronary artery calcification and LAD stent noted.

reports.text:
ULTRASOUND ABDOMINAL AORTA, SCREENING
Indication: Male, former smoker, age 68.
Findings: The abdominal aorta is visualized from the diaphragm to the bifurcation. Normal caliber throughout, measured in the anteroposterior plane. No aneurysm or dissection flap. Common iliac arteries normal in caliber.
reports.conclusion: Normal caliber abdominal aorta. No abdominal aortic aneurysm.

documents.title: CT and ultrasound results

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Office Visit: mood
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here with daughter, who called yesterday.

HPI: Over roughly the last month Paul has pulled away from everything. He hasn't been out to start the garden, which his daughter says is unheard of in March, and he stopped watching football with his neighbor. Most days he is in bed until afternoon. He needs reminding to eat and to shower. He falls asleep fine but is up around 3 in the morning and lies there until it gets light. He describes himself as "tired of everything." Asked directly: no thoughts of suicide, no plan, never attempted, no guns in the house. No hallucinations. Weight down 5 kg in about 3 weeks by our scale. No change in cardiac symptoms, no chest pain, no dyspnea. No new medicines, no alcohol increase (hasn't had a beer in weeks). No prior episodes of depression that he or his daughter can recall. Couldn't name a trigger. He does still walk the dog, briefly, because "she won't let me not."

PHQ-9: 21. Answered item 9 as 0.

Exam: vitals within normal limits, weight as charted. Thin, slumped in the chair, poor eye contact, speech slowed with long latency, flat affect. Oriented, follows the conversation, recall 3/3. Thyroid not enlarged. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no mass. No edema.

Assessment: Major depressive disorder, single episode, severe, without psychotic features: neurovegetative symptoms, psychomotor slowing and weight loss, no SI. Rule out medical contributors.

Plan:
- CBC, CMP, TSH, B12 today.
- Start mirtazapine 15 mg at bedtime: should help sleep and appetite, and sits well with his heart medicines. Reviewed sedation, that benefit takes weeks.
- Offered referral to counseling; he declined for now, "let's see if the pill works." Will revisit.
- Safety: daughter staying over a few nights this week. 988 and our after-hours line given to both. Daughter will text me if anything changes.
- Video check in 2 weeks, visit in 6 weeks. Daily weights not needed; weekly is fine.

55 minutes spent, more than half counseling and coordination.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Paul (and hello to your daughter, who I know reads these). Your blood work came back normal: blood count, kidneys, liver, salts and calcium, thyroid and B12. That is reassuring that nothing physical is driving how you've been feeling. Keep taking the mirtazapine every night. Our video visit is on the 18th.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm with second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I: progressive PR prolongation with intermittently dropped QRS complexes, grouped beating. Ventricular rate 38. Narrow QRS. No acute ST-segment changes.

documents.title: Emergency department physician record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department. Received by fax 04/09/2024. Date of service 04/06/2024.

CC: passed out at home.
HPI: 70M with CAD (LAD stent 2020), HTN, on metoprolol, who went down while walking from the living room to the kitchen this evening. Brief, came to on the floor; no seizure activity, no incontinence, no head strike per patient. Called his daughter, who called EMS. Felt washed out but no chest pain or shortness of breath.
Meds per patient list: aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, mirtazapine nightly, acetaminophen prn.
Allergies: NKDA.
Exam on arrival: pulse 38, BP 88/60, RR 16. Awake and alert, tired looking. Heart sounds distant, no murmur; lungs clear. Remainder of cardiopulmonary exam unremarkable. No injuries.
ECG: Mobitz I second-degree AV block, rate 38.
Labs: hs-troponin I normal x2. Potassium normal. Creatinine normal. Hemoglobin normal.
Course: placed on telemetry with pads on. Metoprolol held. Rate came up to the 50s-60s overnight without intervention; no higher-grade block on telemetry. BP normalized.
Impression: syncope due to symptomatic second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I, likely aggravated by beta blocker.
Disposition: discharged 04/07. STOP metoprolol. Follow up with cardiology within 2 weeks and with PCP this week. Return for recurrent lightheadedness or fainting.

reports.text:
EXERCISE TREADMILL TEST (outside cardiology)
Indication: stable angina, more frequent off beta blocker.
Protocol: Bruce. Baseline ECG: sinus rhythm, normal conduction.
The patient exercised to near-target heart rate and stopped for typical chest pressure at peak exercise. Horizontal ST depression developed at peak and resolved in recovery, along with the chest pressure. Blood pressure response normal. No arrhythmia or conduction abnormality during exercise or recovery.
reports.conclusion: Positive for exercise-induced ischemia with typical angina. No arrhythmia. Findings consistent with his stable angina; elective coronary angiography recommended.

Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40 qhs, lisinopril 20, mirtazapine 30 qhs, acetaminophen prn. No beta blocker. NKDA.
Exam: vitals reviewed. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema. Knees with crepitus, unchanged.
Prevention: LDCT due 11/2024, ordered. Colon UTD. Vaccines: flu and COVID next month; RSV done 2023.
A/P: CAD with worsening stable angina, workup underway with cardiology. MDD partial remission: keep mirtazapine for now given everything going on; he agrees. HTN, lipids: labs today. RTC after cath, then 3 months.

documents.title: Cardiac catheterization procedure note
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology, cardiac catheterization laboratory. Procedure date 09/30/2024. Received 10/03/2024.

Procedure planned: elective left heart catheterization and coronary angiography.
Indication: stable angina with positive exercise treadmill test 09/05/2024; CAD with prior MI and LAD drug-eluting stent (2020).
Pre-procedure: alert, comfortable, no chest pain. No known drug allergies. Home medications: aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, mirtazapine 30 mg, acetaminophen prn. Not on a beta blocker since 04/2024.

Event: Arterial access obtained without difficulty. Shortly after the first contrast injection the patient abruptly became flushed and hypotensive and then obtunded. Temperature 36.9 C, HR 118, BP 78/40, RR 26, SpO2 95% on room air. Tachycardic, skin warm and diffusely erythematous, bounding peripheral pulses. No JVD, no rales, no peripheral edema. No urticaria, no wheeze, no stridor.
Assessment: anaphylactoid reaction to iodinated contrast.
Management: contrast stopped and the procedure aborted before diagnostic images were complete. IV epinephrine, rapid IV fluid boluses, IV diphenhydramine and IV methylprednisolone. Mental status and blood pressure recovered over about 20 minutes. Sheath removed, hemostasis achieved.
Post-procedure: observed overnight on telemetry; no recurrence, no arrhythmia. Discharged 10/01 in good condition.

Plan: iodinated contrast allergy added, severe. Any future contrast study requires steroid and antihistamine premedication with an anesthesia team available. Coronary anatomy not defined; continue medical management of angina for now and review in clinic.

documents.title: Heart cath
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Doc, I guess you heard the cath didn't go well. I had a bad reaction to the dye and they had to stop. They said I'm allergic now. Does that mean no more scans? I have my lung CT next month.

documents.title: RE: Heart cath
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Paul, I read the report and I'm glad you came through it. I've added the contrast dye allergy to your chart as severe. Your lung screening CT uses no dye at all, so that is safe to keep. If you ever need a test with dye in the future it can still be done, with medicines given beforehand to prevent a reaction; always tell anyone doing a scan or a procedure about this allergy. Cardiology will see you to plan next steps for the chest pressure.

documents.body: Flu high-dose L deltoid, 2024-25 COVID R deltoid. New contrast allergy noted on screening, not relevant to these vaccines; no vaccine reactions ever. Observed 15 minutes without issue.

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Ten weeks after the aborted cath (contrast reaction). Fully recovered from that. Chest pressure about weekly with exertion, sometimes twice, always settles with rest within minutes; no rest pain, no syncope, no palpitations. Sees cardiology early January to decide on next steps. Mood good, PHQ-9 5.
Exam: vitals reviewed. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema.
A/P: stable angina, more frequent off beta blocker, cardiology managing; told him to call or go to the ED for chest pain at rest or lasting more than 15 minutes. HTN controlled on lisinopril. Contrast allergy on file. MDD partial remission, continue mirtazapine. RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Office Visit: leg swelling
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: ankles swelling.

HPI: 71 y/o with CAD (prior MI, LAD stent), stable angina, HTN, and the contrast reaction during his aborted cath in September. Cardiology added nifedipine ER 30 mg at his January visit for the angina and pressure; we did not get a note, med rec today from his bottle and the pharmacy. About 3 weeks ago his ankles and feet started swelling. Heavy by evening, shoes tight by supper, almost gone when he gets up. No shortness of breath, no orthopnea, no PND. No chest pain or palpitations lately and the chest pressure is less frequent since nifedipine. No weight gain he's noticed. Hasn't traveled, no diet change, hasn't been laid up.
ROS: no muscle aches, no urinary symptoms, no rash or skin changes, appetite fine, not tired, not dizzy. Sleeping well. Still walks the dog every morning; garden not started yet.

Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40 qhs, lisinopril 20, nifedipine ER 30 (cardiology), mirtazapine 30 qhs, acetaminophen prn. No beta blocker since 4/2024.
Allergy: iodinated contrast, anaphylactoid.

Exam: BP 132/78, other vitals normal. Comfortable. Neck veins flat. Heart regular, no murmur, rub or gallop. Lungs clear, no crackles or wheeze. Abdomen soft, nontender, no hepatosplenomegaly, no ascites, no bruits, normal bowel sounds. Legs: 2+ pitting edema both ankles to mid-shin, symmetric, no redness or warmth, calves soft and non-tender. Reflexes and strength normal.

Data today: ECG normal sinus rhythm. CXR clear, no congestion, heart size normal. Labs drawn: CMP with LFTs, UA.

Assessment: bilateral dependent edema starting weeks after nifedipine, with no sign of heart failure, clot, kidney or liver cause on exam; pending labs, this is calcium channel blocker edema.

Plan:
- Leg elevation in the evening; knee-high compression stockings, prescription given.
- I'd like to talk to his cardiologist before changing the nifedipine, since he is off beta blockers and it seems to be helping his angina. Will call.
- Return precautions: dyspnea, one-sided leg swelling or pain.
- Recheck 3 months.

reports.text: Complete AV dissociation: regular P waves march through without conduction, with a regular junctional escape rhythm at 42. QRS narrow. No acute ST elevation.

Left ventricle normal in size with normal wall thickness. Mild hypokinesis of the inferior wall; remaining segments contract normally. LVEF 50% by biplane method. Right ventricle normal size and function. No significant valvular disease. No pericardial effusion. IVC normal with normal respiratory variation.
reports.conclusion: LVEF 50% with inferior wall hypokinesis. No significant valve disease.

Regional hospital ED. Faxed 04/03/2025. Date of service 04/01/2025.
CC: collapse.
HPI: 71-year-old man with CAD and prior LAD stent, Mobitz I block a year ago, found on the kitchen floor by himself this morning after going down on the way to the kitchen. Brief loss of consciousness. Tired, no chest pain reported.
Home meds per patient list (copied from prior visit): aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, metoprolol succinate 50 mg, nifedipine ER 30 mg, mirtazapine, acetaminophen prn.
Allergies: iodinated contrast (anaphylactoid).
Exam: pulse 42, BP 88/60, RR 16. Alert, fatigued. Distant heart sounds, otherwise unremarkable heart and lung exam. No trauma.
ECG: complete heart block, junctional escape 42.
ED course: transcutaneous pacing pads with capture, then temporary transvenous pacing wire by cardiology. BP improved with pacing. Initial labs sent.
Disposition: admitted to cardiology CCU.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Regional hospital, cardiology service. Admitted 04/01/2025, discharged 04/05/2025. Received 05/02/2025 after records request.

Principal diagnosis: third-degree AV block with syncope.
Secondary: non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction; CAD s/p LAD drug-eluting stent 2020; hypertension; hyperlipidemia; iodinated contrast allergy; depression in partial remission.

Hospital course:
1. Complete heart block: presented with syncope, escape rate 42 and hypotension. Paced transcutaneously then by temporary transvenous wire. Block persisted off all AV-nodal agents. Dual-chamber permanent pacemaker implanted 04/03/2025 via left subclavian approach without complication. Device interrogation at discharge normal.
2. NSTEMI: high-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 1,860 ng/L. Coronary angiography 04/02/2025 after premedication with prednisone and diphenhydramine for his prior contrast reaction; no reaction this time. Patent LAD stent. Moderate diffuse disease of the right coronary and circumflex arteries, no lesion suitable for stenting. Medical therapy. Echo: LVEF 50%, inferior hypokinesis, no significant valve disease.
3. Metoprolol: with pacemaker support, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily restarted for post-MI care.

Discharge medications: aspirin 81 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg nightly; metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily (restarted); lisinopril 20 mg daily; nifedipine ER 30 mg daily; mirtazapine 30 mg nightly; acetaminophen 500 mg q6h prn.
Allergies: iodinated contrast media, anaphylactoid; premedicate.
Instructions: no lifting the left arm above shoulder or more than 10 lb for 4 weeks. Wound check in device clinic 7-10 days. Cardiology follow-up 4-6 weeks. PCP within 1 week.

Regional hospital emergency department. Faxed 10/14/2025. Date of service 10/06/2025.

CC: passed out mowing the lawn.
HPI: 72-year-old man with CAD, NSTEMI in April of this year, prior AV block with a dual-chamber pacemaker since April, brought by EMS. A neighbor saw him go down behind the mower; he was out briefly and woke up weak and dizzy. EMS found him hypotensive with a regular pulse of 160.
Meds: aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol succinate 50 mg, lisinopril, nifedipine ER, mirtazapine, acetaminophen prn.
Allergies: iodinated contrast media (anaphylactoid).
Exam: confused, slow to answer, BP 74/46 and HR 160 despite IV fluid bolus en route and on arrival.
ECG: wide-complex tachycardia, rate 160.
Course: hemodynamically unstable wide-complex tachycardia, treated as VT. Sedated and given one synchronized shock, converting to sinus rhythm with ventricular pacing. Mental status cleared within minutes; BP 108/66. Potassium, magnesium and troponin normal.
Impression: sustained ventricular tachycardia with syncope and shock, 6 months after MI.
Disposition: admitted to cardiology for electrophysiology evaluation and probable defibrillator upgrade. No driving.

documents.body:
Outside cardiology device clinic. Visit 12/04/2025.
History: dual-chamber pacemaker 04/2025 for complete heart block; sustained ventricular tachycardia with syncope 10/06/2025 requiring cardioversion. On 10/09/2025 the pacemaker generator was replaced with a dual-chamber ICD and a defibrillator lead was added, for secondary prevention. (Implant report on file at the hospital.)
Interrogation: normal device function. Lead parameters stable. Battery good. No treated ventricular arrhythmias, no shocks or ATP since implant. Ventricular pacing frequent, as expected.
Incision well healed.
Plan: remote monitoring every 3 months, in-office check in 6 months. Continue metoprolol. Driving restriction through early April 2026.

Regional hospital emergency department. Faxed 03/11/2026. Date of service 03/10/2026.

CC: left flank pain, dizzy.
HPI: 72-year-old man with CAD, prior MIs, ICD, who had an outpatient diagnostic cardiac catheterization yesterday for unstable angina via the left femoral artery, discharged home last evening. Around 4 this morning he had a sudden onset of severe left flank pain and felt dizzy when he stood. Arrived about 2 hours after onset.
Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, nifedipine ER 30, mirtazapine 30, acetaminophen prn.
Allergies: iodinated contrast media (anaphylactoid) - premedicated for yesterday's procedure.
Exam: BP 90/50, HR 110. Pale and sweaty. Abdomen soft; tender in the left flank, no guarding or rebound, no peritoneal signs. Left groin access site with small bruise, no expanding hematoma, distal pulses present.
Labs: hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL; pre-procedure hemoglobin yesterday 14.0 g/dL.
Bedside ultrasound (ED): no free intraperitoneal fluid.
ECG: no new changes compared with prior (paced).
CT abdomen and pelvis WITHOUT contrast (contrast allergy): left retroperitoneal hematoma along the psoas, about 9.4 x 6.1 cm. No intraperitoneal blood.
Impression: retroperitoneal hematoma after femoral catheterization, with hypotension responding to fluids.
Plan: IV fluids, type and screen, serial hemoglobin, hold aspirin, bed rest. Admit to medicine with cardiology following.

Regional hospital emergency department. Faxed 04/09/2026. Date of service 04/07/2026.

CC: rectal bleeding.
HPI: 72-year-old man with CAD and prior MIs, ICD, on aspirin, recently admitted for a retroperitoneal hematoma after catheterization, now with 2 hours of severe cramping abdominal pain and several bloody bowel movements, bright red. Pale and sweaty on arrival.
Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, nifedipine ER 30, mirtazapine 30, acetaminophen prn.
Allergies: iodinated contrast (anaphylactoid).
Exam: BP 95/60, HR 110, RR 22. Abdomen soft, mild tenderness throughout, no rebound or guarding. Rectal: bright red blood.
Labs: Hgb 8.2, Hct 24.5, platelets 220, INR 1.0, creatinine 1.1, BUN 29.
Assessment: brisk GI bleed with hemodynamic compromise. BUN out of proportion to creatinine favors an upper source.
ED management: two large-bore IVs, crystalloid, IV pantoprazole bolus and infusion, aspirin held, 1 unit packed red cells ordered. GI consulted for endoscopy.
Disposition: admitted, step-down unit.

documents.title: Upper endoscopy report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Regional hospital endoscopy unit. Procedure date 04/08/2026. Received 04/13/2026.
Indication: hematochezia with hemodynamic instability and elevated BUN; suspected upper GI bleed.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care.
Findings: Esophagus normal. Stomach normal; biopsies taken from antrum and body for H. pylori. Duodenal bulb: 1 cm ulcer with a non-bleeding visible vessel, no active bleeding. Second portion of the duodenum normal.
Therapy: dilute epinephrine injected around the vessel; two hemostatic clips placed with good result.
Impression: duodenal bulb ulcer with non-bleeding visible vessel, treated endoscopically.
Recommendations: high-dose PPI, then pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily for 8 weeks followed by once daily while on aspirin. Follow biopsies. Resume aspirin in 3 days if no rebleeding, per cardiology. GI clinic in 6-8 weeks.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital. Admitted 04/07/2026, discharged 04/10/2026.

Principal diagnosis: upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage from a duodenal bulb ulcer.
Course: presented with hematochezia, BP 95/60 and HR 110, hemoglobin 8.2. IV pantoprazole. Transfused 1 unit packed red cells given his coronary disease, hemoglobin 8.9 afterward. EGD 04/08: 1 cm duodenal bulb ulcer with visible vessel, injected and clipped. No rebleeding. Gastric biopsies negative for H. pylori. Aspirin held for 3 days and restarted 04/10 after discussion with cardiology. Hemoglobin 9.3 at discharge.

Discharge medications: NEW pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily for 8 weeks, then 40 mg once daily. Continue aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40, metoprolol succinate 50, lisinopril 20, nifedipine ER 30, mirtazapine 30, acetaminophen prn. Avoid NSAIDs.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week with CBC; GI clinic 6-8 weeks.

documents.title: Gastroenterology clinic letter
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside gastroenterology clinic. Visit 05/28/2026.
Dear colleague,
Mr. Pelletier returns after his April admission for a bleeding duodenal bulb ulcer, treated with epinephrine and clips. Gastric biopsies were negative for H. pylori; the ulcer is attributed to aspirin. No further bleeding, normal stools, no dyspepsia.
Medications include aspirin 81 mg and pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily.
Allergies: iodinated contrast.
Exam: well, abdomen soft and nontender.
Plan: complete the twice-daily course this week, then pantoprazole 40 mg once daily long-term for as long as he takes aspirin. A duodenal ulcer with H. pylori-negative biopsies does not need a repeat endoscopy. Avoid NSAIDs. We are happy to see him again if needed.
